tagline: Above downtown Pittsburgh, the byway links overlooks and surviving hillside inclines.
intro: Grand View Scenic Byway takes in Pittsburgh’s Grandview Avenue, P.J. McArdle Roadway and Sycamore Street. Visit Pennsylvania highlights its views of downtown and access to the Mount Washington overlook and two inclines. The corridor became a Pennsylvania byway in 2003. At its western end, Grandview Avenue reaches the edge of Mount Washington at Point of View Park.

Reaching this hillside was once a problem for the people who lived on it. In the 1860s, industry occupied most of the flat ground along the Monongahela’s south bank, pushing housing onto Mount Washington’s steep slopes. German immigrants proposed cable inclines, and the Monongahela passenger line opened in 1870. As roads multiplied and car use grew in the twentieth century, most inclines closed; by the late 1960s, only the Monongahela and Duquesne remained in operation. The 2003 road designation also supplied the former name of Grand View Scenic Byway Park, now Emerald View Park.

For an east-to-west sequence of stops, begin with the Monongahela Incline and continue to the Duquesne Incline, where an observation deck faces Pittsburgh’s Golden Triangle. Finish at Grandview Avenue and Sweetbriar Street, the byway’s westernmost end. There, Point of View Park holds a bronze sculpture of George Washington and Seneca leader Guyasuta meeting face to face.

moments.title: Monongahela Incline
moments.text: The Monongahela Incline began as an answer to a steep commute. German immigrants living on Mount Washington proposed cable cars like those they remembered from their former country. John Endres designed the line with assistance from his daughter Caroline, and it opened for passengers on May 28, 1870. A larger freight incline opened beside it in 1884 and operated until 1935. That neighboring line could carry vehicles as well as people; its concrete pylons remain visible during the passenger incline’s descent. The passenger line is one of two survivors from seventeen passenger-carrying inclines in Pittsburgh.

moments.title: Duquesne Incline
moments.text: The Duquesne Incline closed in 1962 with major repairs needed and few passengers. Duquesne Heights residents raised money to restore it, and a nonprofit reopened the line on July 1, 1963. Samuel Diescher’s incline had been completed in 1877, originally powered by steam. Its later refurbishment exposed the original wood of the cars built by Philadelphia’s J. G. Brill and Company. An observation deck at the top overlooks the Golden Triangle, pairing the restored cars with the city view. The line rises 400 feet at an angle of 30 degrees along Mount Washington.
moments.notice: The restored cars show their original wood beneath the removed paint.

moments.title: Point of View Park
moments.text: George Washington and Seneca leader Guyasuta face one another with their weapons lowered in James A. West’s bronze Point of View. Installed in 2006, the sculpture depicts their October 1770 meeting, when Washington was examining land for future settlement along the Ohio River. The parklet takes its name from the artwork. It occupies Mount Washington’s edge at Grandview Avenue and Sweetbriar Street, marking the westernmost end of the byway above the cityscape. Before Mayor Luke Ravenstahl dedicated the park in October 2006, the concrete overlook drew visitors photographing the city below.
moments.notice: The two bronze figures face each other with their weapons lowered.
